name: Desktop
description: Desktop computing — the machines people actually sit in front of. Its two big families, Linux and the BSDs, share a Unix heritage but differ in kernel, licensing and governance.

children.name: Linux
children.description: An operating system kernel started by Linus Torvalds in 1991 and released under the GPLv2. Around it grew the largest open-source ecosystem: it runs most of the world's servers, every Android phone, and a sizeable share of desktops.

children.name: Init Systems
children.description: The first process the kernel starts, plus the machinery that brings services up and supervises them afterwards. The choice of init shapes how a distribution boots and how daemons are managed.

children.name: systemd
children.description: The dominant init system and service manager, introduced by Lennart Poettering in 2010. It handles boot, services, timers and logging through journald — powerful, and often criticised for how much it absorbs.

children.name: runit
children.description: A minimal init and process-supervision suite. Small, fast and easy to reason about; it is the default init in Void Linux.

children.name: s6
children.description: A supervision suite by Laurent Bercot, built from small, composable tools. Favoured by distributions such as Artix and Obarun that want supervision without systemd.

children.name: openrc
children.description: A dependency-based init system used by Gentoo and Alpine Linux. It keeps the classic SysV-style script model while adding proper dependency handling.

children.name: Distros
children.description: A distribution bundles the Linux kernel with a package manager, a userland and sensible defaults. Distributions are how people actually install and run Linux.

children.name: Debian
children.description: A community-run distribution founded in 1993, known for stability and a strict free-software policy. It is the base for Ubuntu, Linux Mint and countless others.

children.name: apt
children.description: Debian's package manager, and the tool nearly every Debian-derived distribution uses to install and upgrade software. It resolves dependencies over .deb packages.

children.name: Fedora
children.description: Red Hat's fast-moving community distribution. New upstream technology lands here first and later flows into Red Hat Enterprise Linux. Software is packaged as RPMs.

children.name: rpm
children.description: The RPM Package Manager: a package format and toolchain from Red Hat, used by Fedora, RHEL and openSUSE. This node is shared — the same tooling shows up in two different ecosystems.

children.name: dnf
children.description: Fedora's package manager and the successor to yum. It resolves dependencies and installs RPM packages, leaning on the libsolv solver in recent versions.

children.name: openSUSE
children.description: A community distribution backed by SUSE, notable for its YaST administration tool and the Tumbleweed rolling release. It packages software as RPMs too.

children.name: zypper
children.description: openSUSE's package manager. It installs RPM packages and integrates with the distribution's repositories, patterns and system rollback.

children.name: BSD
children.description: The Berkeley Software Distribution family: free Unix-like systems descended from the original Unix. Each project ships its kernel and userland together as one coherent operating system.

children.name: Distros
children.description: The BSD projects are complete operating systems rather than kernels with a bolted-on userland, so the distribution and the operating system largely coincide.

children.name: FreeBSD
children.description: A general-purpose BSD with a reputation for performance and networking. Common on servers and appliances — Netflix uses it for content delivery.

children.name: pkg
children.description: FreeBSD's binary package manager. It installs prebuilt packages quickly, and can also drive builds from the Ports collection.

children.name: OpenBSD
children.description: Focused on security and correctness, with a famously thorough audit of its code. It gave the world OpenSSH and the PF firewall.

children.name: pkg_add
children.description: OpenBSD's package tool. pkg_add installs prebuilt binary packages from the project's official mirrors and pkg_delete removes them; the Ports tree builds the same software from source.

children.name: NetBSD
children.description: Portability above all — it runs on more hardware architectures than any other operating system, and keeps a clean, well-structured codebase while doing it.

children.name: pkgin
children.description: A binary package manager for pkgsrc with an apt-style interface, and the usual way to install prebuilt packages on NetBSD.

children.name: Windows
children.description: Microsoft's proprietary desktop operating system. Not open source itself, but it runs a great deal of it — which is what the package managers below are for.

children.name: winget
children.description: Microsoft's own package manager, formally the Windows Package Manager. It installs from a community-maintained catalogue of manifests and ships with recent versions of Windows.

children.name: chocolatey
children.description: A long-standing package manager for Windows, built on the NuGet packaging format. It predates winget and has a very large community repository.

children.name: scoop
children.description: A command-line installer for Windows aimed at developers. It installs into a per-user directory, so it never needs administrator rights.

children.name: macOS
children.description: Apple's proprietary desktop operating system, and a common home for open-source developer tooling — most of which arrives through Homebrew.

children.name: homebrew
children.description: The package manager most macOS developers use. It installs command-line tools and graphical applications, and runs on Linux too.

children.name: Applications
children.description: Open-source programs that run on the desktop regardless of which operating system sits underneath them.

children.name: Office
children.description: Suites for documents, spreadsheets and presentations — the category where open source became a practical alternative to Microsoft Office.

children.name: libreoffice
children.description: The Document Foundation's office suite: word processor, spreadsheet, presentations, drawing and databases. Shipped by most Linux distributions, and a direct descendant of OpenOffice.org.

children.name: onlyoffice
children.description: An office suite with unusually high Microsoft Office format fidelity, and a self-hosted collaboration server. Its editors are also embedded in Nextcloud and similar platforms.

children.name: openoffice
children.description: Apache OpenOffice, the suite LibreOffice forked from in 2010. Development has since slowed to a crawl, and most of its users have moved to LibreOffice.

children.name: Media
children.description: Players and editors for video and audio.

children.name: vlc
children.description: VideoLAN's media player. It plays practically any format without extra codecs, on virtually every platform, and is one of the most-installed open-source programs there is.

children.name: mpv
children.description: A minimalist, keyboard-driven media player descended from MPlayer. Scriptable, and favoured by people who would rather configure playback in a file than click through menus.

children.name: shotcut
children.description: A cross-platform non-linear video editor built on FFmpeg. It supports a wide range of formats with no import step.

children.name: kdenlive
children.description: KDE's non-linear video editor, with multi-track editing and a broad effects set. One of the most mature open-source options for editing video.

children.name: Graphics
children.description: Tools for images, drawing and illustration.

children.name: GIMP
children.description: The GNU Image Manipulation Program: a free raster image editor for photo retouching, drawing and format conversion. Around since 1996, and still the flagship open-source alternative to Photoshop.

children.name: Browsers
children.description: Programs for browsing the web.

children.name: firefox
children.description: Mozilla's browser, and for years the main counterweight to Internet Explorer and Chrome. Gecko is the only major browser engine not controlled by Google or Apple.

children.name: librewolf
children.description: A privacy-hardened fork of Firefox: telemetry removed, tracking protections tightened, and no sponsored content. Maintained independently of Mozilla.

children.name: helium
children.description: A lightweight Chromium-based browser that strips out Google's services and telemetry while keeping the engine. Much newer and smaller than the established alternatives.

children.name: brave
children.description: A Chromium-based browser built around blocking ads and trackers by default. It funds itself through its own ad programme and a crypto token.

children.name: Mail
children.description: Email clients.

children.name: thunderbird
children.description: Mozilla's email, calendar and news client. Like Firefox, it moved under a separate corporation so that it could fund its own development.

children.name: Security
children.description: Password managers, and the servers that can back them.

children.name: keepassxc
children.description: A cross-platform password manager that keeps your database in a local file you own. It reads the KeePass format, so other clients can open the same vault.

children.name: bitwarden
children.description: An open-source password manager with both hosted and self-hosted options. Popular with teams because the clients, server and audit tooling are all open.

children.name: vaultwarden
children.description: An unofficial, resource-light reimplementation of the Bitwarden server in Rust. Most Bitwarden clients work against it, which makes self-hosting cheap.

children.name: File sharing
children.description: Peer-to-peer and file transfer tools.

children.name: qbittorrent
children.description: A BitTorrent client with a deliberately plain interface and a built-in web UI. One of the most widely used clients on Linux.

children.name: Editors
children.description: Terminal text and code editors.

children.name: vim
children.description: Bram Moolenaar's vi improved, a modal editor found on nearly every Unix system. Its keybindings are so widespread that other tools imitate them.

children.name: neovim
children.description: A refactor of Vim that moves it forward with asynchronous plugins, Lua configuration and an embeddable core. Popular enough that many users now treat Vim as the legacy option.

children.name: helix
children.description: A modal editor written in Rust, with multiple selections as a first-class idea and language servers built in. Configuration is TOML rather than a scripting language.
